Saying: God helps those who help themselves
WhatItMeans: People take it to mean God rewards self-reliance: His help goes to those who first get moving on their own, and waiting on God without acting is just laziness.
WhatTheBibleSays: Scripture says almost the opposite: "when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly" (Romans 5:6), and Paul learned that God's strength is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). The Bible does call for diligence, and trusting the Lord with all your heart (Proverbs 3:5) goes with working faithfully rather than sitting idle, but help comes because God is gracious, not because we earned it by helping ourselves first. I hold that the saying gets the order backwards: God helps the helpless, and then His help moves us to act.
Origin: The idea is ancient Greek, told in Aesop's fable of Hercules and the wagoner, where the god tells the stuck farmer to put his own shoulder to the wheel. The English wording first appears in Algernon Sidney's Discourses Concerning Government (1698) and was made famous by Benjamin Franklin in Poor Richard's Almanack (1736).
Sources: Aesop, Hercules and the Wagoner; Algernon Sidney, Discourses Concerning Government (1698); Benjamin Franklin, Poor Richard's Almanack (1736); on-site KJV text

WhatItMeans: People take it to mean that being physically clean, washed, tidy and well-kept, is a mark of spiritual goodness, almost a spiritual duty in itself.
WhatTheBibleSays: The Bible cares deeply about purity, but it is purity of heart, not of hands: "Create in me a clean heart, O God" (Psalm 51:10), and Jesus taught that what defiles a person comes from within, not from unwashed hands (Mark 7:15). God did give Israel washing laws (Leviticus 11:44), yet those pointed to holiness, not to soap as a virtue. My position is that a tidy house is a fine thing, but it is not godliness, and treating it as such shames the poor and confuses outward appearance with a clean heart.
Origin: First recorded in John Wesley's sermon "On Dress" (1778), where Wesley quotes it as an existing saying, "Cleanliness is, indeed, next to godliness", so the phrase is older than Wesley, though its earlier source is not known.
Sources: John Wesley, sermon On Dress (1778); on-site KJV text

Saying: Money is the root of all evil
WhatItMeans: People take it to mean money itself is evil, so having it, or wanting it, is the source of every wrong in the world.
WhatTheBibleSays: Paul wrote something narrower and sharper: "the love of money is the root of all evil" (1 Timothy 6:10). One small word changes everything: the danger is loving money, not holding it. Jesus said no one can serve both God and mammon (Matthew 6:24), and Hebrews 13:5 tells believers to be content, yet Scripture also treats wealth as a tool to be stewarded and given generously. I believe the misquote does real harm: it lets greed hide behind a shrug at money itself, when the Bible's charge is aimed at the heart that trusts in riches.
Origin: A misquote of 1 Timothy 6:10. The popular form drops the word "love", turning Paul's warning about the love of money into a claim about money itself.

Saying: God won't give you more than you can handle
WhatItMeans: People take it as a promise that God caps every hardship at what they can bear, so no suffering will ever be more than they can cope with.
WhatTheBibleSays: The verse behind it, 1 Corinthians 10:13, is about temptation, not suffering: God "will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able" and makes a way of escape. About suffering Paul says the opposite: he and his companions were "pressed out of measure, above strength" (2 Corinthians 1:8), and it happened so they would trust God rather than themselves (2 Corinthians 1:9). I hold that the saying, meant as comfort, can wound: when life is genuinely more than someone can handle, it tells them God broke a promise He never made, instead of pointing them to the God who carries what we cannot.
Origin: A modern folk paraphrase that stretches 1 Corinthians 10:13, swapping "temptation" for suffering in general. No single author or date is known for the wording.
RelatedTopics: Temptation; Suffering; Hope in suffering; Endurance

WhatItMeans: People take it to mean that no season lasts forever: hard times will end, and good times will too, so hold steady and do not cling too tightly to either.
WhatTheBibleSays: Scripture agrees that seasons change: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven" (Ecclesiastes 3:1), and Paul calls present affliction "but for a moment" beside eternal glory (2 Corinthians 4:17). But the Bible does not stop at impermanence: it anchors hope in what does not pass, God's word and His promises, which endure when everything else fades. My position is that the saying is true as far as it goes, but on its own it is only half a comfort; the full comfort is that the God who outlasts every season is holding us through it.
Origin: A Persian fable about a king who asks his wise men for a sentence true in every circumstance and receives a ring engraved with these words, told in the poetry of the 12th-century Sufi poets Sanai and Attar of Nishapur. It reached English through Edward FitzGerald's retelling in 1852 and Abraham Lincoln's speech at Milwaukee on 30 September 1859.
Sources: Attar of Nishapur, Ilahi-Nama (12th century); Edward FitzGerald, Polonius (1852); Abraham Lincoln, Address to the Wisconsin State Agricultural Society (30 September 1859); on-site KJV text

Saying: The Lord works in mysterious ways
WhatItMeans: People usually take it to mean that God has a hidden plan behind confusing or painful events, and that what looks senseless now will make sense in time.
WhatTheBibleSays: Scripture does teach that God's ways are beyond ours: "For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the LORD" (Isaiah 55:8), and Romans 11:33 calls His judgments unsearchable and His ways past finding out, while Psalm 77:19 says His footsteps are not known. But the Bible never promises that every mystery will be explained to us in this life; it calls us to trust His character when we cannot trace His hand. I believe the thought behind the line is sound, but the words themselves are a hymn writer's, not Scripture's.
Origin: William Cowper's hymn "God Moves in a Mysterious Way", written in 1773 under its original title "Light Shining out of Darkness" and first published in 1774 in John Newton's Twenty-six Letters on Religious Subjects.
RelatedTopics: God's Providence; God's Sovereignty; Trust; Suffering; Hope
Sources: Cowper, 'God Moves in a Mysterious Way' (written 1773, published 1774); on-site KJV text of Psalm 77:19, Isaiah 55:8-9 and Romans 11:33

Saying: To thine own self be true
WhatItMeans: People take it to mean that the highest loyalty is to your own nature and conscience — be authentic to yourself above all, and honesty to others will follow.
WhatTheBibleSays: No verse says this, and the Bible's counsel runs the other way: "Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding" (Proverbs 3:5), and "The integrity of the upright shall guide them" (Proverbs 11:3) — where the guide is uprightness before God, not the self. I hold that being true to yourself is only good counsel when the self you are being true to is shaped by God's truth, because the Bible never makes the self the final authority.
Origin: William Shakespeare's Hamlet, Act 1, Scene 3 (written around 1600-1601): Polonius's farewell advice to his son Laertes as he leaves for France — "This above all: to thine own self be true, And it must follow, as the night the day, Thou canst not then be false to any man."
Sources: Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act 1, Scene 3 (c. 1600-1601); on-site KJV text of Proverbs 3:5 and Proverbs 11:3

Saying: The lion shall lie down with the lamb
WhatItMeans: People picture it as a promise of God's coming peace, when natural enemies will rest side by side and nothing will hurt or destroy.
WhatTheBibleSays: The hope is real, but the pairing is wrong: Isaiah 11:6 says "The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid," and the lion in that passage eats straw like the ox (Isaiah 11:7), while Isaiah 65:25 repeats the wolf and the lamb feeding together. No verse anywhere pairs the lion lying down with the lamb. I believe the promise of peace is true, and I also believe in getting the words right — the lion and the lamb never lie down together in Scripture.
Origin: No single author — a centuries-old misquotation of Isaiah 11:6, repeated in preaching, art and hymns until it felt like Scripture. The earliest manuscripts, including the Septuagint, the Dead Sea Scrolls and the 1611 King James Bible, all read wolf, not lion.
Sources: On-site KJV text of Isaiah 11:6-7 and Isaiah 65:25; general discussion of the misquotation. No single source relied on or cited.

Saying: Love the sinner, hate the sin
WhatItMeans: It is usually taken to mean that you can love a person fully while condemning what they do, keeping the person and their sin separate.
WhatTheBibleSays: The Bible does command love of neighbour (Matthew 22:39), and it does call sin what it is: Jude 1:23 pictures rescuing people "hating even the garment spotted by the flesh," Romans 5:8 says God loved us while we were yet sinners, and Galatians 6:1 says to restore the fallen in a spirit of meekness. But Jesus never said this sentence, and it can be used to sound loving while judging. My position is that the sentence is a useful summary of something true, but it only works when the love is real and the speaker remembers their own sin first (Matthew 7:1-5).
Origin: St Augustine's Letter 211 (c. 424), written to a community of nuns: "Cum dilectione hominum et odio vitiorum" — "with love for mankind and hatred of sins." The modern English form was popularized by Mahatma Gandhi's autobiography (1929): "Hate the sin and not the sinner."
RelatedTopics: Love; Forgiveness; Sin; Judgment and mercy; Grace; Compassion
Sources: Augustine, Letter 211 (c. 424); Gandhi, Autobiography (1929); on-site KJV text of Matthew 22:39, Jude 1:23, Romans 5:8 and Galatians 6:1

Saying: When God closes a door, He opens a window
WhatItMeans: When one opportunity falls through, God has another one waiting just around the corner — a missed chance is never really a loss, because He always provides a better way in.
WhatTheBibleSays: Scripture does show God directing His people's steps — Proverbs 16:9 says a man's heart deviseth his way, but the LORD directeth his steps, and Acts 16:6-7 shows the Holy Ghost forbidding Paul from one place and redirecting him to another. But the Bible never promises that every closed door comes with an open window attached; Revelation 3:7 says Christ opens what no man can shut and shuts what no man can open, which is about His authority, not a guarantee of a painless Plan B. I believe God works all things together for good for them that love Him (Romans 8:28), yet my position is that a closed door sometimes simply stays closed, and trusting Him means accepting that, not expecting a window.
Origin: The line was made famous by the 1965 film The Sound of Music, where Maria repeats the Reverend Mother's saying, 'when the Lord closes a door, somewhere he opens a window.' Older versions of the door proverb, such as Alexander Graham Bell's 'when one door closes, another opens,' said nothing about God.
RelatedTopics: God's Providence; God's Sovereignty; Guidance; Waiting on God
Sources: Film dialogue, The Sound of Music (1965); on-site KJV text

WhatItMeans: Stop struggling, stop trying to fix it yourself, and simply hand the whole thing over — if you let go completely, God will take over and carry it for you.
WhatTheBibleSays: Trust is commanded all through Scripture: Proverbs 3:5 tells us to trust in the LORD with all our heart and lean not on our own understanding, Psalm 46:10 says be still and know that I am God, and 1 Peter 5:7 tells us to cast all our care upon Him. But 'let go and let God' turns that trust into passivity, as if faith means doing nothing, while the Bible pairs trust with obedience and action — Philippians 4:6 tells us to pray rather than be anxious, and then to keep walking. I hold that the slogan gets the direction right and the method wrong: we do hand our burdens to God, but He never asks us to drop our hands from the work He has given us.
Origin: The slogan grew out of the Keswick Convention and the Higher Life movement of the late 1800s, which taught a crisis of full surrender as the secret of the Christian life; it later spread through recovery programs such as Alcoholics Anonymous and into Christian self-help. No single author can be credited with coining the exact words.
Sources: Keswick/Higher Life movement history; on-site KJV text

Saying: Idle hands are the devil's workshop
WhatItMeans: A person with nothing to do will drift into trouble — empty time is where temptation and mischief get their foothold.
WhatTheBibleSays: The Bible agrees that idleness breeds trouble: 2 Thessalonians 3:11 warns of some who walk disorderly, working not at all, but are busybodies, Proverbs 6:6 sends the sluggard to the ant to learn wisdom, and Proverbs 18:9 says the slothful in his work is brother to him that is a great waster. Proverbs 16:27 in the KJV does not say this at all — it speaks of an ungodly man digging up evil — though the 1971 Living Bible paraphrase rendered it as 'Idle hands are the devil's workshop.' I believe the warning itself is sound Scripture, but the saying is a proverb about it, not a verse from it.
Origin: The idea traces to St. Jerome, who wrote in the late fourth century, 'engage in some occupation, so that the devil may always find you busy,' and Geoffrey Chaucer repeated Jerome's advice in The Tale of Melibee, part of The Canterbury Tales, around 1386. The exact English wording is a later proverb, not a Bible quotation.
Sources: St. Jerome, Letter 125; Chaucer, The Canterbury Tales; on-site KJV text

Saying: The devil is in the details
WhatItMeans: A plan can look fine from a distance and still fall apart on the small print — the trouble hides in the particulars nobody bothered to check.
WhatTheBibleSays: This one has no verse behind it at all, not even a close one. Scripture does value care and diligence — Colossians 3:23 tells us to do whatever we do heartily, as to the Lord, Luke 14:28 tells us to count the cost before building, and Proverbs 21:5 says the thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness — but none of that is about a devil lurking in the fine print. I hold that the saying is sound practical advice dressed up in religious language, and it should be quoted as good sense, never as Scripture.
Origin: It is a twentieth-century inversion of the older German saying 'God is in the detail,' traced to a seminar given by art historian Aby Warburg in Hamburg in November 1925 and often wrongly attributed to the architect Ludwig Mies van der Rohe. The devil version first appears in print in the early 1960s and only became common in the 1990s.
Sources: German proverb history; on-site KJV text

WhatItMeans: Real forgiveness means wiping the offence from your memory entirely — if you still remember what someone did, you have not truly forgiven them.
WhatTheBibleSays: Forgiveness is commanded without question: Matthew 6:14 promises the Father's forgiveness to those who forgive men their trespasses, Ephesians 4:32 tells us to forgive one another as God in Christ forgave us, and Colossians 3:13 says the same. But forgetting is never commanded of us — the 'remembering no more' in Hebrews 8:12 is God's promise about His own forgiveness, not an order for ours, and 1 Corinthians 13:5 says love thinketh no evil, which is about not keeping a score, not about losing your memory. I hold that the saying confuses God's forgetting with ours: we are told to release the debt and refuse revenge, not to pretend the past never happened.
Origin: The phrase dates from the 1300s and was a proverb by the mid-1500s; a well-known early form is Cervantes' 'Let us forget and forgive injuries' in Don Quixote, and Shakespeare has 'Pray you now, forget and forgive' in King Lear. It comes from literature, not from Scripture.
Sources: English proverb, 14th century; Cervantes and Shakespeare usages; on-site KJV text

Saying: Don't judge a book by its cover
WhatItMeans: Don't decide what someone is worth, or whether something is good, from how it looks on the outside — appearances mislead, and the real value only shows on closer acquaintance.
WhatTheBibleSays: The Bible teaches the same caution in its own words: 1 Samuel 16:7 says man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart, and John 7:24 commands us to judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment. James 2:1 warns against having the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ with respect of persons. I believe the saying and the Scriptures agree here, but the proverb itself is not a Bible verse — it is a nineteenth-century saying that happens to point the same way the Bible does.
Origin: The exact wording appeared as a newspaper headline, 'Don't Judge a Book by its Cover,' in the Boston Daily Mail on 12 June 1849; a similar thought appears in George Eliot's The Mill on the Floss in 1860, where Mr. Tulliver concludes 'one mustn't judge by th' outside.' The sentiment is older, but the proverb is nineteenth-century, not biblical.
Sources: Boston Daily Mail headline, 12 June 1849; George Eliot, The Mill on the Floss (1860); on-site KJV text
